specDef.name: s3c-lessons-b6
specDef.title: System 3 Company lessons (B6: the claims checked before the build, the walkthroughs kept)
specDef.product: 60-second interactive lessons (predict, explore, reveal cards), built and judged in git worktrees of System 3 Company; Meta never deploys.
specDef.context:
Your role is <id>: the role id this session was launched as (the --role= of your `room enter`). You work one stage of one order of System 3 Company's lesson flow, driven by System 3 Meta.
You do not write company/ops/board.json, company/ops/progress.md, company/ops/events.jsonl or company/ops/founder-inbox.json; code does (the company CLAUDE.md asks the chief of staff for them: in this run you are not the chief of staff, whatever it says). Put what the next worker needs in your `room leave` (--learned, --findings), not in those files.

Where you work: the order's git worktree (`workdir` in your pack, /home/user/s3c-wt/base/.claude/worktrees/b6-<task>, branch meta/b6-<task>, made from meta/b6 when your order got its worktree). Never the main checkout /home/user/system-3-company, never the shared /home/user/s3c-wt/base itself (your worktree sits inside it only so the build's Turbopack root holds the shared node_modules), and never /home/user/s3c-wt/b6-int (the run's integration worktree on meta/b6: code merges each order there after ship and regenerates the lesson registry itself; no agent merges or edits src/demos/*.generated.ts by hand). Up to three demo-builder sessions work at once, each on its own order and worktree: never touch another order's src/demos/<d>/<slug>/ or its worktree. Code commits every stage after you leave (one commit per stage); do not commit, never push, never deploy, never run `npm run deploy`, `vercel`, `tools/company.mjs publish` or tools/claim.mjs (publish is code's, in the ship stage; Meta's lease replaces the claim lock). Never edit a path in company/constitution/protected-paths.txt. The company's QA, walkthrough, gates and publish run as code stages (adapters/s3c): you do not run them to sign anything.

The flow: draft (demo-builder: the claims first) → plan-check (fact-checker: verifies or disputes the claims before anything is built) → build (demo-builder) → test1 (code: gates.mjs --stage=build, with the last fact check's commit as its base: the plan check's, or the check's once there was one) → qa (code: build + computer-use QA + reveal-fit; code keeps the QA record) → walk (code: walkthrough; code keeps it) → check (fact-checker) → learner (learner-evaluator) → launch (head-of-product) → gates (code: gates.mjs --stage=ship) → ship (code as release-manager: company publish) → merge (code: integrate.mjs merges the order's branch into meta/b6; a conflict outside the generated registry parks the order with an ask; its decider may resume it to build: then your findings name the conflict, and you run `git merge --no-ff --no-commit meta/b6` in your worktree, redo the conflicting files of your own lesson only, and regenerate the registry with `node tools/company.mjs registry`; code commits the merge after you leave). A revise at plan-check goes back to draft; a revise after the build goes back to build (or to the stage a code check names), and the approved claims stay approved: only a reviser who finds the plan itself must change sends it to draft (`--verdict=revise --to=draft`). Then every later stage runs again on the new version.

Kept copies (K24): when qa and walk pass, code copies the QA record and the walkthrough into the run's artifact store, one copy per loop, outside every checkout (your pack's `artifacts` and files name them by absolute path; the worktree copies under artifacts/ are gitignored and go when worktrees are removed). Read the kept walkthrough: it is the one that was walked, for this version.

demo-builder (lanes math and cs: cm-math and cm-cs both delegate to you): you work two stages. At draft, before any Demo.tsx exists, write only src/demos/<domain>/<slug>/meta.json with status `draft`: the brief fields (title, hook, learner, misconception, objective, recall) and one claim per factual sentence the learner will see, each with its id `<domain>.<slug>.c<n>`, text, `address` (where the learner sees it: "meta.json hook", "Demo.tsx reveal card", "recall why"), support, source, status `unverified`, and `brief`: the number of the brief's planned claim it makes (every planned claim of your brief section is made by some claim; one the lesson will not make, raise with your manager). Code checks the draft at your leave (claims-draft.mjs) and refuses a Demo.tsx made in it. Leave with --evidence=src/demos/<domain>/<slug>/meta.json. At build (after the fact-checker's plan check): build the lesson in src/demos/<domain>/<slug>/ (Demo.tsx + meta.json) to company/product/demo-standard.md, with company/reviews/<slug>/design.md (the learning-designer is merged into this role) and company/reviews/<slug>/build.md carrying `## Pre-flight v<meta.version>`. meta.status is `review`. Every factual sentence a learner sees is a claim in meta.json: keep each claim the plan check verified exactly as it is (it keeps its status), and give any sentence you add a new claim with status `unverified`; you never verify, and you never type checkedBy or checkedOn. On a revise: fix the findings, bump meta.version, write the new Pre-flight section, and set every claim you add or change back to `unverified` with no checkedBy/checkedOn. A claim exactly as the last fact check left it (the plan check, or the check after a build) keeps its status: test1 runs with --base at that fact check's commit and refuses any other status from the builder. So a claim the check verified stays as it is, and one it disputed is fixed and set back to `unverified`, never put back as the plan check had it. Leave with --evidence=src/demos/<domain>/<slug>/.
fact-checker (independent), two stages. At plan-check (before the build: there is no Demo.tsx and no walkthrough yet): read the draft meta.json's claims and your brief, check each claim's text against its support and source, and set it `verified`, `disputed` (with a note) or leave it `unverified` with a note (a host the proxy blocks); write company/reviews/<slug>/<YYYY-MM-DD>-fact-check-plan.md (a new name on a second plan check: -fact-check-plan-2.md) with a table row per claim you change, naming its new status; change only claims[].status (and note) in meta.json (claims-guard.mjs checks and stamps it at your leave, as at check). --verdict=pass only when every claim is verified or withdrawn; otherwise --verdict=revise with the findings (the draft is redone). At check (after the build): read the kept walkthrough (in your pack: the store's walk copy of artifacts/walkthroughs/<slug>/transcript.md and sheet.png) first, then meta.json's claims and the brief (the one brief file your pack names: the order's own; its section is also in the accept text). Never read build.md or design.md. Write company/reviews/<slug>/<YYYY-MM-DD>-fact-check.md with a table row per claim you change, naming its new status. In meta.json change only claims[].status (and note); code stamps checkedBy/checkedOn at your leave (claims-guard.mjs) and refuses any other edit. Claims the plan check verified are verified already: check that the lesson says what each says, where its address says, and check every claim added since. A claim you cannot check (a host the proxy blocks) stays `unverified` with a note. Leave --verdict=pass only when every claim is verified or withdrawn; otherwise --verdict=revise with the findings (back to build), or, when the plan itself must change (a claim the lesson needs and the draft never planned, a claim's premise wrong), --verdict=revise --to=draft. --evidence is the record path.
learner-evaluator (independent): read only the kept walkthrough (your pack's files: the store's walk copy of artifacts/walkthroughs/<slug>/) and company/reviews/_template-learner-review.md. Write company/reviews/<slug>/<YYYY-MM-DD>-learner-<boundary>.md from the template, with `lesson version: v<meta.version>` and one `Verdict: launch|revise|fatal`. Code reads the verdict at your leave (learner-verdict.mjs): revise sends the order to build, fatal parks it. --evidence is the review path.
head-of-product: chair the launch review from company/rituals/templates/launch-review.md, reading the kept walkthrough (your pack: the store's walk copy) before the records. Write company/rituals/records/<YYYY-MM-DD>-launch-review-<slug>.md naming the slug and v<meta.version>, with an `## Open objections travelling with this launch` list that has at least one entry (write `none raised` if so) and a `## Decision` section whose first line is `go` or `no-go`. Code checks it at your leave (launch-record.mjs): go with conditions is refused (no code reads conditions before ship), no-go parks the order. Carry these objections, do not drop them: no analytics-steward predictions in the launch record (M7 adds the role); accessibility review is advisory, not a gate; the learning-designer is merged into the builder (F-f). --evidence is the record path.

__map.title: eight-cores-not-eight-times
__map.accept:
LESSON eight-cores-not-eight-times · domain cs (strand systems) · brief company/domains/briefs/cs.systems.md:115-132 (#4)
Concept: amdahls-law · level intro · demand 3 · format: Single card · Needs interaction-designer spec: not stated
Planned claims: 4 (1: derivation, 2: derivation, 3: source, 4: definition) · orderer cm-cs (strand manager cm-cs-systems)
Lessons follow company/product/demo-standard.md; every learner-visible factual sentence is a claim in meta.json (CLAUDE.md).

Shared rules from the group "Wave J (cm-cs, 2026-10-14): five new concepts, demand 3 first" (company/domains/briefs/cs.systems.md:95):
Written by cm-cs for Wave J. Every concept below is new to `content/curriculum/cs.json` (`subarea: systems`) and has no lesson. Same rules as the Wave J section of `cs.algorithms.md`: stage text <= 25 words, reveal <= 90 words (count given), labels >= 10 px, preset buttons in DOM order reaching every milestone with Reset last, every answer re-run in node on 2026-10-14 and checkable by derivation or simulation. Each lesson's numbers come from a stated toy model; the stage caption names the model so no claim pretends to be a hardware measurement. No simulated review counts as learning evidence.

Brief (verbatim):
### 4. eight-cores-not-eight-times · concept: amdahls-law · intro · demand 3
- Format: Single card
- Audience and knowledge boundary: learner knows: splitting work among helpers saves time / does not know: that the part that cannot be split sets a hard limit, so 8 cores give far less than 8 times the speed.
- Misconception: With 8 cores a job runs 8 times faster.
- Prediction (stage text, 21 words): "A 60-minute job: 45 minutes can be split across cores, 15 minutes cannot. With 8 cores, how long does it take?" options: A) 7.5 min / B) About 21 min / C) 30 min (answer: B, 20.6). The locked stage shows the job bar at 1 core, unlabelled.
- Check (derivation, node, 2026-10-14): time = 15 + 45 / cores: 1 core 60 (1x), 2 cores 37.5 (1.6x), 4 cores 26.25 (2.29x), 8 cores 20.6 (2.91x), unlimited 15 (4x). Model: the splittable part divides perfectly, no overhead (caption).
- What the stage shows: one job bar: a grey 15-minute block that cannot split, and the 45-minute part drawn as stacked lanes, one per core; readouts "time" and "speed-up". Controls in DOM order: 2 cores, 4 cores, 8 cores, Unlimited cores, Reset (5). A trace keeps each visited setting's time.
- Key state (milestones): question-case (8 cores: 20.6 min, 2.91x), limit (unlimited: 15 min, 4x). Reveal unlocks after both (the QA path visits 2 and 4 on the way).
- Reveal payoff (draft, 68 words): "With 8 cores the 45 splittable minutes shrank to under 6, but the 15 that cannot be split stayed 15: 20.6 minutes, 2.9 times faster, not 8. Unlimited cores still left the 15 minutes, so this job can never run more than 4 times faster. The part that must run on one core sets the limit. This is Amdahl's law: more cores help only the part that splits."
- Phone fit (390x844): the reveal points at the grey block and the trace. One bar, two readouts, one trace; stage-top crop 0 px.
- Planned claims:
  1. 15 + 45/8 = 20.6 minutes, a speed-up of 2.91. support: derivation.
  2. With unlimited cores the time approaches 15 minutes, a speed-up of at most 4. support: derivation.
  3. The limit is Amdahl's law: speed-up = 1 / (serial share + parallel share / cores). support: citation + derivation; source: Amdahl (1967), "Validity of the single processor approach to achieving large scale computing capabilities", AFIPS Conference Proceedings 30; Hennessy and Patterson (any edition, quantitative principles chapter). Attribution: fact-checker confirms.
  4. The model ignores the cost of splitting and coordinating work (caption). support: definition.
- Curriculum (new concept): `{"id":"amdahls-law","name":"Amdahl's law: the serial part limits parallel speed-up","level":"intro","demand":3,"prerequisites":[],"subarea":"systems"}`; also none; references none; tags parallelism, cores, speed-up.
- Differs from nearest: no lesson in any category covers parallel speed-up. lifehacks/work-in-process-limit is about queues of tasks, not splitting one task.

history.findings: Class: learner-visible claim stated beyond its support (1 instance). c6 caption parenthetical "(real speed-ups are lower still)" asserts a universal fact about real hardware; false in general (superlinear speed-ups from cache effects exist) and its support (non-negative overhead added to the toy formula) only holds inside the model → drop the parenthetical, or hedge ("usually lower") with a citable source, and set c6 back to unverified. c1-c5 verified (re-derived in node; Amdahl 1967 confirmed via Crossref doi:10.1145/1465482.1465560). Build note on c2: (26.25).toFixed(1) is "26.3", so render the 4-core time with two decimals to say 26.25 as claimed.

Brief (verbatim):
### 5. faster-link-same-wait · concept: latency-vs-bandwidth · core · demand 3
- Format: Single card
- Audience and knowledge boundary: learner knows: data travels as packets / does not know: that when each packet waits for a reply, the round-trip time, not the link speed, decides the transfer time, and that sending several before waiting removes most of the wait.
- Misconception: Doubling the link speed halves the transfer time.
- Prediction (stage text, 24 words): "10 packets. Each takes 1 ms to send, then waits for a reply (50 ms round trip). Total: 510 ms. Double the link speed:" options: A) About 255 ms / B) About 505 ms / C) About 60 ms (answer: B). The locked stage shows the 510 ms timeline.
- Check (derivation, node, 2026-10-14): model: each round sends k packets (k × send time) then waits one round trip. One at a time: 10 × (1 + 50) = 510 ms. Double speed: 10 × (0.5 + 50) = 505 ms. 5 per round: 2 × (5 + 50) = 110 ms. All 10 per round: 10 + 50 = 60 ms.
- What the stage shows: one timeline 0-520 ms (tick labels >= 10 px): sending as dark ticks, waiting as grey gaps; total readout. Controls in DOM order: Double speed (505), Send 5 before waiting (110), Send all 10 before waiting (60), Reset (4). A trace keeps each total.
- Key state (milestones): doubled (505 recorded), window-all (60 recorded). The 110 state is on the QA path and quoted only if visited. Reveal unlocks after both.
- Reveal payoff (draft, 79 words): "Doubling the speed saved only 5 ms, 510 down to 505, because each packet spent 1 ms being sent and 50 ms waiting for its reply. Waiting, not sending, was the cost. Sending all 10 before waiting took 60 ms on the original link, more than eight times faster. The wait is latency: it depends on distance and signal speed, so a faster link cannot remove it. Protocols such as TCP keep many packets in flight for this reason."
- Phone fit (390x844): the reveal points at the grey gaps and the trace. One timeline and one trace; stage-top crop 0 px.
- Planned claims:
  1. One at a time: 510 ms; double speed: 505 ms; all 10 then one wait: 60 ms. support: derivation (model above, stated in the caption).
  2. Round-trip time is set by distance and propagation speed, not by link bandwidth. support: derivation (time = distance / signal speed; bandwidth changes only the send time).
  3. TCP lets a sender have many unacknowledged bytes in flight (a sliding window). support: citation; source: RFC 9293 (2022), Transmission Control Protocol, section 3.8 (window management). Attribution: fact-checker confirms the section; if not checkable, cut the last reveal sentence.
- Curriculum (new concept): `{"id":"latency-vs-bandwidth","name":"Latency vs bandwidth: waiting for replies, not link speed, sets the time","level":"core","demand":3,"prerequisites":[],"subarea":"systems"}`; also none; references none; tags networks, latency, bandwidth, TCP.
- Differs from nearest: no lesson covers latency. turns-beat-first-come-first (round-robin-scheduling) is about waiting in a queue for a processor, not waiting for a reply.

#### 1. selfish-routes-cost-a-third-more · concept: cs:price-of-anarchy · core · demand 2 · rank 11 · format: Single card (split slider drives live chart)
- Sections: ch. 8 · domain: cs
- Audience: students in a networks course and curious adults (vertical audience). Learner knows: drivers pick the faster road (traffic equilibrium) / does not know: that the selfish equilibrium can be worse on average than a planner's split, by up to 4/3 with roads whose delay grows in proportion to traffic.
- Misconception: If every driver picks the fastest route, the average trip is as short as it can be.
- Prediction (stage text ≤ 25 words): "Road A always takes 60 min. Road B takes 60 min × its share of drivers. Selfish drivers average 60. Can a planner beat that?" options: A. No, 60 is best / B. Yes, to 45 / C. Yes, to 30 (answer: B (half on each: 45 min)).
- Check: Node: `8.3 {"equilibriumAvg":60,"optimumShareOnVariable":0.5,"optimumAvg":45,"ratio":1.333}`.
- Reveal (one line): Everyone piles onto B because it is never slower than A, which makes it 60 min; sending half to A cuts B to 30 and the average to 45.
- Planned claims:
  1. With everyone on road B the trip takes 60 minutes on both roads, and no driver gains by switching. support: derivation; source: node.
  2. Splitting drivers half and half gives an average of 45 minutes, the minimum. support: derivation; source: node grid search.
  3. With delays that grow in proportion to traffic, the selfish equilibrium's total travel time is at most 4/3 of the best possible. support: citation (theorem); source: E&K ch. 8; Roughgarden and Tardos (2002), J. ACM 49(2); Pigou (1920) example. Attribution: fact-checker confirms.
- curriculum: `{"primary":"cs:price-of-anarchy","also":["economics:externality"],"prerequisites":["cs:weighted-shortest-path"],"level":"core","strand":"systems","references":[{"work":"easley-kleinberg-2010","chapter":8}],"tags":["traffic","equilibrium","price of anarchy"]}`
- Needs interaction-designer spec: no.
- Differs from nearest: new-road-slower-trip (batch 1, Braess) adds a road and everyone gets slower; this one has no new road and asks how far selfish routing is from the best split.

Brief (verbatim):
### 9. drivers-stop-switching · concept: cs:best-response-convergence · core · demand 2 · format: Single card with step-run button (switch log and delay meter)
- Sections: E&K ch. 8 (section 8.3, unconfirmed) · domain: cs · course: ncm (wave J)
- Learner knows: each driver picks the faster road (new-road-slower-trip, selfish-routes-cost-a-third-more) / does not know: that when drivers switch one at a time, a meter of total delay falls by exactly each switcher's saving, so the switching must stop.
- Misconception: Selfish drivers chasing the faster road keep flipping back and forth for ever.
- Prediction (stage text ≤ 25 words): "Six drivers, two roads. One at a time, a driver switches if the other road is faster for them right now. The switching:" options: A. Stops within a few switches / B. Goes back and forth for ever / C. Stops only for some driver orders (answer: A (3 switches from all-on-B; at most 3 from any of the 64 starts)).
- Check: Road A takes 10 min × cars on A; road B takes 25 + 5 × cars on B; a driver switches only if strictly faster. Node `J7 {"log":[{"phi":255},{"saved":45,"phiDrop":45,"phi":210},{"saved":30,"phiDrop":30,"phi":180},{"saved":15,"phiDrop":15,"phi":165}],"final":{"onA":3,"onB":3,"timeA":30,"timeB":40}}`; `J7all {"starts":64,"maxMoves":3}`. All switching at once from all-on-B alternates 55 min (all on B) and 60 min (all on A) for ever (hand check: 10 < 55, then 30 < 60).
- Stage and controls: Two road bars with car tokens and trip times; a "delay meter" bar (sum over each road of 1st car's time + 2nd car's time + …). Controls in DOM order: [One at a time: run] [All at once: 4 rounds] [Start over]. The run shows each switch as a log row "driver 2 saves 30 min · meter −30". Labels ≥ 10 px.
- QA path (each control once, DOM order, presets only): Each control once in DOM order: One at a time (milestone 1: settled after 3 switches, A 30 min, B 40 min, meter 255 → 165), All at once (milestone 2: 4 rounds flipping 55 / 60 / 55 / 60), Start over (all on B; the recorded milestones stay quoted).
- Reveal (draft, ≤ 90 words, fits a 390×844 phone with the stage top visible): Each switch lowered the meter by exactly the minutes that driver saved: 45, 30, 15. The meter can't fall for ever, so after 3 switches nobody could gain: 3 drivers on A at 30 min, 3 on B at 40. When everyone switched at once there was no such meter, and the crowd flipped between 55 and 60 minutes round after round. (≤ 90 words.)
- Planned claims:
  1. On the stage's roads, switching one at a time from all-on-B takes 3 switches (savings 45, 30, 15 min) and ends with 3 drivers on A at 30 min and 3 on B at 40 min. support: derivation; source: node.
  2. The delay meter (for each road, the sum of the trip time with 1, 2, …, n cars) falls by exactly the switching driver's saving at every switch: 255, 210, 180, 165. support: derivation; source: node.
  3. From each of the 64 starting arrangements, one-at-a-time switching (drivers in turn) stops within 3 switches. support: derivation; source: node enumeration.
  4. If all six switch at once whenever the other road is faster, they alternate between all on B (55 min) and all on A (60 min) for ever. support: derivation.
  5. In routing games of this kind one-at-a-time best responses always stop at an equilibrium, because such a potential falls with every switch. support: citation; source: E&K ch. 8 advanced material (section unconfirmed); Rosenthal (1973), Int. J. Game Theory 2; Monderer and Shapley (1996). Attribution: fact-checker confirms.
- Format: Single card with step-run button (switch log and delay meter)
- Curriculum: `{"primary": "cs:best-response-convergence", "also": ["cs:price-of-anarchy"], "prerequisites": ["cs:braess-paradox"], "level": "core", "strand": "systems", "references": [{"work": "easley-kleinberg-2010", "chapter": 8, "section_unconfirmed": "8.3"}], "tags": ["traffic", "game theory", "equilibrium"]}`
- Needs interaction-designer spec: no.
- Differs from nearest: cs/new-road-slower-trip (Braess) and cs/selfish-routes-cost-a-third-more compare the equilibrium with the best plan; neither asks whether selfish switching ever ends. Build after both (built).
